environmentalPersistence: High — tetracycline binds to soil particles and persists months to years; among the most environmentally persistent antibiotics

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate to strong — tetracycline inhibits plant protein synthesis (chloroplasts and mitochondria have prokaryotic ribosomes which tetracycline targets)
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Strong — tetracycline specifically targets chloroplast ribosomes (prokaryotic origin); directly impairs chloroplast protein synthesis
morphologicalEffects.pigmentation: Moderate — antibiotic stress induces defense pigmentation
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: New leaves most affected — actively synthesizing chloroplast proteins; chlorosis appears first on young leaves

physiologyEffects.chlorophyllReduction: Strong — 40–65%; direct mechanism via chloroplast ribosome inhibition

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate to strong — impaired chloroplast function leads to photo-oxidative stress

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Very strong — tetracycline is a broad-spectrum antibiotic; among the strongest microbiome disruptors in the entire 40-chemical library
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Severely suppressed — all tetracycline-sensitive bacteria killed; only resistant strains survive
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Bacterial disruption shifts community toward fungal dominance; mycorrhizal associations disrupted
microbiomeEffects.rhizosphereStability: Severely destabilized — most dramatic microbiome effect in the simulator

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: 3–6 weeks — tetracycline persists in soil; microbiome recovery is the slowest component
temporalDynamics.sensitization: None for plant; but surviving microbiome develops resistance

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Young leaves chlorotic (distinctive young-leaf pattern from chloroplast ribosome inhibition) + moderate purple pigmentation
visualSimulation.firstAffectedRegion: Youngest leaves — diagnostic for tetracycline vs most other chemicals
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Young-leaf chlorosis + purple tint + microbiome collapse — the most distinctive combined plant/microbiome signature in the pharmaceutical group
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate amber-purple — anhydrotetracycline and anthocyanin signature; distinctive of antibiotics
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Near-zero diversity — most dramatic microbiome collapse in simulator; only resistant cluster remains; resistome particles dominant
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Plant partial recovery in weeks; microbiome recovery takes months — long-lasting ecological damage even after plant improvement

synergies.synergyNote: The pharmaceutical pollutant quartet — antibiotic + NSAID + stimulant + analgesic co-contamination in wastewater-irrigated soils. Antibiotics provide the resistome amplification that makes the mixture uniquely dangerous — resistant pathogens that survive the antibiotic thrive in the NSAID/stimulant-disrupted microbiome.

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Livestock agriculture (60–80% of antibiotics globally used in animals; excreted into manure and soil), hospital wastewater, pharmaceutical manufacturing, human sewage — found in agricultural soils on every continent
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Not approved for crop use — massive contamination from livestock manure applied as fertilizer; most commercially used antibiotics in agriculture are tetracyclines
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Low at environmental concentrations; antibiotic resistance crisis is the primary human health concern — not direct toxicity but resistance gene selection
educationalContext.climateLink: Antibiotic resistance is not directly linked to climate but antibiotic-resistant pathogen spread is worsened by climate-driven migration and extreme weather events affecting sanitation
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Environmental — livestock and hospital waste; pharmaceutical manufacturing runoff
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Antibiotic resistance is predicted to kill 10 million people per year by 2050 — more than cancer. Livestock antibiotic use is a primary driver. The food students eat connects directly to one of the most serious medical crises in human history.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Antibiotic resistance crisis, livestock antibiotic use, pharmaceutical pollution, one health framework
